name: Turbo Pascal
title: Turbo Pascal: structured programming on DOS
intro: Turbo Pascal was Borland's Pascal for CP/M and DOS, first released in 1983. It was fast and cheap, and it came with an editor, compiler and debugger in one blue screen, so for a decade it was how a great many people learned to program, at school and at home. Pascal itself was designed by Niklaus Wirth to teach structured programming: declare everything first, keep blocks clearly nested, and let the compiler catch type mistakes. Turbo Pascal grew into Borland Pascal and then into Delphi, whose courses are in this learner too. These lessons use Turbo Pascal 7 style. Every example is a whole program and shows exactly what it prints. To run one today, use Free Pascal (fpc -Mtp hello.pas), or the original IDE in a DOS emulator such as DOSBox.

lessons.title: Your first program
lessons.summary: program, begin ... end., Write and WriteLn, comments.

sections.p: A Pascal program has a name, then a block between begin and end. (with a full stop at the very end). Statements are separated by semicolons. WriteLn prints its items and ends the line; Write prints without ending it. Comments go between { } or (* *).
Pascal ignores upper and lower case in keywords and names, so WRITELN, writeln and WriteLn are the same. Strings are written with single quotes, and a quote inside a string is doubled.

practice.why: Write does not end the line, so A, B and C all land on one line, and WriteLn ends it.
Everything between { and } is a comment.
Inner blocks end with end; but the main block ends with end. and the compiler stops reading there.
Borland released it in 1983. Its line continued as Borland Pascal and then Delphi.

lessons.title: Variables and types
lessons.summary: var blocks, Integer, Real, Char, Boolean, and field widths.

sections.p: Every variable is declared in a var section before begin. Assignment is :=, and = is only for comparing. / always gives a Real; div and mod are whole-number division and remainder.
sections.out:
Hazel has 17 nuts
3 each, 2 left over

sections.p: In Write and WriteLn, x:8 prints x right-aligned in 8 characters, and for a Real, x:8:2 also sets 2 digits after the point. This is how Pascal programs lined up columns of numbers. Always give a Real a width; without one it prints in scientific notation.

On DOS, Integer is only 16 bits, from −32768 to 32767. Go past the top and it wraps round to the bottom without any warning, unless range checking is switched on with {$R+} and {$Q+}. Use LongInt (32 bits) for bigger numbers.

practice.why: div gives the whole number of times 5 fits into 17, and mod gives what is left.
A width of 3 right-aligns the number in three characters, padding with spaces on the left.
/ always gives a Real, and :0:2 prints it with exactly two decimals and no padding.
A 16-bit Integer wraps at both ends: one below −32768 is 32767.

practice.q: What is the difference between := and = in Pascal?
practice.why: Pascal keeps them apart on purpose, so if X = 1 can never accidentally change X.

lessons.title: Decisions and loops
lessons.summary: if, case, for, while and repeat ... until.

sections.p: if ... then ... else picks between two statements. To run several statements, wrap them in begin ... end. There is no semicolon before else. case picks by value, with ranges written 1..5.

for I := 1 to 3 do counts up, and downto counts down. while checks before each pass, so it may not run at all. repeat ... until checks after each pass, so it always runs at least once, and it needs no begin ... end.

practice.why: repeat checks its condition after the body, so the body runs once even though N > 3 is already true.
A case label can list several values. 'e' is one of them.

practice.q: Why does if X > 1 then WriteLn('a'); else WriteLn('b'); not compile?
options: There must be no semicolon before else
WriteLn cannot be used in if
X must be declared as Boolean
practice.answer: There must be no semicolon before else
practice.why: The semicolon ends the if statement, so the compiler then finds an else with no if.

lessons.title: Procedures and functions
lessons.summary: Declaring them before use, var parameters and nesting.

sections.p: Procedures and functions are declared before the main begin. A function returns its value by assigning to its own name. Parameters are copied in by default; mark one var and the procedure works on the caller's variable instead.

Pascal lets you declare a procedure inside another one. The inner procedure can use the outer one's variables and is invisible everywhere else, which keeps helpers close to the only place they are used.

practice.why: X is a copy of N because it is not a var parameter, so N is unchanged.
With var, X is N itself, so each call adds 10 to it.

practice.q: How does a Turbo Pascal function return its value?
options: By assigning to the function's own name
With the result of the last line
practice.answer: By assigning to the function's own name
practice.why: Square := N * N sets the result. Delphi later added the Result variable as well.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.summary: Short strings, Length, Copy, Pos, Concat and the length byte.

sections.p: A Turbo Pascal string holds up to 255 characters, and string[10] holds at most 10; anything longer is cut off. Characters are numbered from 1. Length, Copy(S, Start, Count), Pos(Sub, S) and + or Concat cover most needs, and UpCase capitalises one character.

A short string stores its length in position 0, as a character, followed by the text. Ord(S[0]) is the same as Length(S). Old programs sometimes set S[0] directly to shorten a string, which is fast but easy to get wrong.

practice.why: Copy starts at position 3 (characters count from 1) and takes 4 characters.
string[3] holds at most three characters, so the rest is cut off.
z is the third character, and Pos returns 0 when the text is not found. The two numbers are printed side by side.

practice.q: What is the longest a plain Turbo Pascal string can be?
practice.why: The length is kept in one byte at position 0, so it can't go above 255.

lessons.title: Arrays, records and sets
lessons.summary: Typed arrays with any range, records, enumerations and sets.

sections.p: An array's index range is part of its type, and it can start anywhere: array[1..5], array[0..9] or array['A'..'Z']. A record groups named fields, and with lets you use the fields without repeating the record's name.

An enumerated type lists its own values, and Ord gives each value's position, counting from 0. A set holds any group of values of a small type, and in tests whether a value is in it. Sets make checks like "is this a vowel?" short and fast.
sections.out:
2 is busy
e is a vowel

practice.why: The array is indexed 5 to 7, so A[6] is the middle element, set to 6 × 2.
Enumerated values count from 0: Red is 0, Green 1, Blue 2.
4 is in the set and 5 is not.

lessons.title: Units and the DOS screen
lessons.summary: uses Crt, writing your own unit, and the IDE.

sections.p: This lesson is reading material: the Crt unit needs a DOS text screen, so the examples show no output here.

uses Crt; gives a program control of the text screen: ClrScr clears it, GotoXY(X, Y) moves the cursor, TextColor and TextBackground pick from 16 colours, ReadKey waits for a key without echoing it, and Delay pauses for some milliseconds. Menus, games and the famous blue-and-yellow screens of the era were built this way.

A unit is a separately compiled module. Its interface part lists what other programs may use, and its implementation part holds the code. Change the implementation and the programs that use it do not need to change.

Turbo Pascal's IDE kept the editor, compiler and debugger in one program. F9 compiles, Ctrl+F9 runs, F7 and F8 step through the code a line at a time, and Ctrl+F7 adds a watch on a variable. Compiling took seconds even on slow machines, which is a big part of why it was loved.

practice.q: What does the interface part of a unit contain?
practice.why: The interface is the public list. The code itself goes in the implementation part.

practice.q: Which unit gives ClrScr and GotoXY?
practice.why: Crt handles the text screen and keyboard. Dos has file and system calls, and Graph draws in graphics modes.

practice.q: What did Turbo Pascal's line eventually become?
practice.why: Borland Pascal with Objects was followed by Delphi in 1995. Lazarus is a later, separate project built on Free Pascal.

lessons.title: Text files
lessons.summary: Assign, Rewrite, Reset, Append, ReadLn and Close.

sections.p: A Text variable is a text file. Assign ties it to a path, Rewrite creates or replaces it, Reset opens it for reading, and Close finishes. WriteLn(F, ...) writes a line; ReadLn(F, ...) reads one. Eof(F) is true when there is nothing left to read. Parsing a line of words often means ReadLn into a string, then Pos, Copy and Val.
Append opens an existing text file so new WriteLn calls add at the end. After writing, close it and Reset again if you need to read the whole log back.

practice.why: Write prints without a newline, so x and y land on one line.
Append adds elm after the line already written by Rewrite.

options: Ties a file variable to a path, without opening it yet
practice.answer: Ties a file variable to a path, without opening it yet
practice.why: Rewrite, Reset or Append is what actually opens the file.

practice.q: What does Val(S, N, Code) do?
options: Converts text S into number N; Code is 0 when it worked
practice.answer: Converts text S into number N; Code is 0 when it worked
practice.why: Val is the Turbo Pascal way to parse a number from a string.

lessons.title: Pointers and linked lists
lessons.summary: New, Dispose, ^ and a short chain of records.

sections.p: A pointer type is written ^T: it holds the address of a T. New(P) allocates one on the heap and points P at it; P^ is the value itself; Dispose(P) frees it. Linked structures use a pointer field inside a record. Always dispose what you new, in reverse order for a chain, or the heap leaks — on DOS that mattered quickly.
Notice PNode = ^TNode before TNode is fully defined. Pascal allows that so a record can contain a pointer to its own type. nil means "no node", and is how the list ends.

practice.why: P^ is the Integer on the heap, set to 9.
A^.Next is B, so A^.Next^.N is B's N.

practice.q: What does nil mean for a pointer?
options: It is the same as Dispose
practice.why: nil is the empty pointer value. Dispose frees memory; it does not by itself assign nil unless you do.

options: Allocates a value on the heap and points P at it
practice.answer: Allocates a value on the heap and points P at it
practice.why: New is heap allocation. The matching free is Dispose.

lessons.title: Objects
lessons.summary: Turbo Pascal object types, methods and Init.

sections.p: From Turbo Pascal 5.5, an object type holds fields and methods (procedures and functions declared inside the type). Method bodies are written later as TypeName.MethodName. You call them with a dot on a variable of that object type. This is the OOP style that led toward Delphi; it is not yet the later class model.
A plain var S: TStash lives like a record: no New needed. You can also allocate objects dynamically with New when you want polymorphism and virtual methods; that is a step further than this lesson.

practice.why: Inc runs twice, so N goes from 2 to 4.
Init sets 0, then two Tick calls add 10 each.

practice.q: How is a method body named?
practice.why: TStash.Add tells the compiler which object type the method belongs to.

practice.q: How does Turbo Pascal object differ from a later Delphi class?
options: object is the older TP model; Delphi's class is reference-based with constructors
practice.answer: object is the older TP model; Delphi's class is reference-based with constructors
practice.why: These lessons stay with object, which Turbo Pascal 7 understands.

lessons.title: Project: a nut ledger
lessons.summary: Enums, event records and a small stock report.

sections.p: A ledger of six events updates a stock array indexed by nut kind. Each event is a record with a kind (found, ate or gift), a nut and a count. Applying an event either adds stock, subtracts it, or prints skipped when there are not enough nuts — the same shape as the inventory projects in the other courses, in Turbo Pascal 7 style.
Load the events from a text file with Reset and Val, store the stock in an object with Apply as a method, or keep the events in a linked list of pointers.

options: The gift asks for 5 but only 3 are in stock
practice.answer: The gift asks for 5 but only 3 are in stock
practice.why: Found adds 3 walnuts; Gift 5 fails the Stock >= Count check.

practice.q: What is the final acorn count?
practice.why: Start 0, found 8, ate 2, gift 1 leaves 5.
Acorn drops by 2; Walnut is untouched.
